\section{Introduction\protect 
%
}\begin{frame}{Secular Stagnation }
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Today: }Can we explain \emph{secular stagnation} through
the lens of heterogeneous agent models?\vfill
\item <+->\textbf{Central economic questions:}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Why have real interest rates fallen since the 1950s?
\item What role did aging and rising inequality play?
\item What happens next, and what does it mean for public debt?\vfill
\end{enumerate}
\item <+->\textbf{Plan for today:}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Income inequality and saving (Straub 2019)
\item The race between asset supply and asset demand (Auclert, Malmberg, Rognlie and Straub 2025)
\item Indebted demand (Mian, Straub and Sufi 2021)
\end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Secular Stagnation}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Secular stagnation}: A state in which private demand is structurally
low 
\begin{itemize}
\item Low level of growth in the economy 
\item Low interest rates 
\item Low level of inflation 
\end{itemize}
\item Large literature suggests that advanced economies have been in this
state over the past $\approx$ 20 years
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Declining interest rates}

Various interest rates from Mian, Straub and Sufi (2021)

\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth]{figs/MSSRates.png}      
\end{figure}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Declining growth}

\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth]{figs/TrendGrowth.png}      
\end{figure}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Rising saving rates and declining $r$}

  Mankiw (2022) writes a simple Solow model to think about secular stagnation \pause
\begin{itemize}
  \item Recall that, on the BGP $r=\alpha \frac{n+g+\delta}{s}-\delta$  \pause 
  \item An increase in savings implies $dr/ds = -\alpha \frac{n+g+\delta}{s^{2}}<0$ \pause
  \item Assume $\alpha=1/3$, $n=0.01$, $g=0.02$, $\delta=0.05$, $s=0.24$, this yields $dr/ds = -0.46$ p.p. \pause
  \item But population and GDP growth have declined as well! $dr/d(n+g) = 1.39$ p.p. \pause
\end{itemize}
Other potential culprit: rising markups. \\ \pause 
Implications for fiscal and monetary policy? Low $r$ means more likely to hit ZLB and fiscal stimulus cheap and powerful.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Explanations}

Large literature on potential explanations
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Increases in market power of firms 
\begin{itemize}
\item Liu, Mian \& Sufi (2022), Aghion, Bergeaud, Boppart, Klenow \& Li
(2023)
\end{itemize}
\item <+->Declining relative price of investment (/reduced innovation)
\begin{itemize}
\item Eichengreen (2015), Eggertsson, Mehrotra \& Robbins (2019)
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Aging population (Demographics)}
\begin{itemize}
\item Auclert, Malmberg, Martenet \& Rognlie (2024), Gagnon, Johannsen \&
López-Salido (2021)
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Increasing income inequality }
\begin{itemize}
\item Straub (2019), Mian, Straub \& Sufi (2021), Auclert \& Rognlie (2020)
\end{itemize}
\item <+->All of these in one framework: Auclert, Malmberg, Rognlie \& Straub (2025)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%

\section[Inequality and saving]{Inequality and saving \\ Straub (2019)}
\begin{frame}{Secular stagnation and income inequality}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->A literature explains the decline in $r$ through \emph{rising} income/wealth
\textbf{inequality }
\begin{itemize}
\item See e.g. Mian, Straub and Sufi (2021): \emph{What explains the decline
in r{*}? Rising income inequality versus demographic shifts}
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Example}: If saving rates increase with income (richer
save more) then:
\begin{itemize}
\item Redistribution from poor to rich households \emph{increase} the aggregate
supply of savings $\Rightarrow$ lower rates in GE
\item Suggests link between increasing income inequality and secular stagnation 
\item Straub (2019, WP) tests this hypothesis 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Stylized model}

\begin{itemize}
  \item Deterministic model with one-period lived households \pause
  \item Constant wage $w$, return $R$ \pause
  \item Get utility from consumption $c_t$ and wealth $a_{t+1}$ \pause 
\end{itemize}
$$\begin{aligned}
\max_{c_t,a_{t+1}} u(c_t)+\beta U(a_{t+1}) \\
c_t +R^{-1} a_{t+1}\leq a_t + w_t   
\end{aligned}$$
with $u(c)=\frac{c^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}$ and $U(a)=\frac{a^{1-\Sigma}}{1-\Sigma}$ \\ \pause
We can show that $c_t \approx k(a_t+w)^\phi$, with $\phi=\frac{\Sigma}{\sigma}$
\end{frame}


%
\begin{frame}{Empirical estimate}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->We can check in the data the empirical relationship between permanent income and consumption
\item <+->If $\phi<1$ consumption rises \emph{less} than proportionally
with income
\begin{itemize}
\item I.e. savings rise \emph{more $\Rightarrow$ }Richer HHs save more 
\item Opposite for $\phi>1$
\end{itemize}
\item <+->Two questions
\begin{itemize}
\item What does this elasticity look like empirically?
\item If $\phi\neq1$ how can we accommodate this in a HA model?
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Empirical estimate}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Use US panel survey data (PSID)
\item <+->Regress $\log c_{it}$ on controls (year, age, HH size, location)
and 9 year average of income
\item <+->Binned scatter:\\
\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.5\linewidth]{figs/Straub2019Scatter.PNG}      
\end{figure}
\item <+->More detailed estimates in paper, suggest $\phi\approx0.7$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Permanent redistribution in the canonical HA model}
\begin{itemize}

\item <+->Consider standard HA model with permanent income state $p:$
\[
\begin{aligned}V\left(a_{t-1},z_{t},p\right)= & \max_{c_{t}}\frac{c_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}+\beta\mathbb{E}\left[V\left(a_{t},z_{t+1},p\right)\right]\\
 & \text{ subject to }\\
 & c_{t}+a_{t}=Ra_{t-1}+z_{t}p\\
 & a_{t}\geq0\\
\ln z_{t} & =\rho\ln z_{t-1}+\epsilon_{t}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item <+->Note: preferences are \emph{homothetic }(homogeneous of degree
1)
\begin{itemize}
\item >>Scale independent<<
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

%
\begin{frame}{Homothetic household problem I}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Normalize constraints by $p$ and Bellman by $p^{1-\sigma}$
\[
\begin{aligned}\frac{V\left(a_{t-1},z_{t},p\right)}{p^{1-\sigma}}= & \max_{c_{t}}\frac{\frac{c_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}}{p^{1-\sigma}}+\beta\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[V\left(a_{t},z_{t+1},p\right)\right]}{p^{1-\sigma}}\\
 & \text{ subject to }\\
 & \frac{c_{t}}{p}+\frac{a_{t}}{p}=R\frac{a_{t-1}}{p}+z_{t}\frac{p}{p}\\
 & \frac{a_{t}}{p}\geq\frac{0}{p}
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Homothetic household problem II}
Define $\tilde{c}_{t}=\frac{c_{t}}{p}$,$\tilde{a}_{t}=\frac{a_{t}}{p}$,$\tilde{V}_{t}=\frac{V_{t}}{p^{1-\sigma}}$
to get:
\[
\begin{aligned}\tilde{V}\left(\tilde{a}_{t-1},z_{t}\right)= & \max_{\tilde{c}_{t}}\frac{\tilde{c}_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}+\beta\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{V}\left(\tilde{a}_{t},z_{t+1}\right)\right]\\
 & \text{ subject to }\\
 & \tilde{c}_{t}+\tilde{a}_{t}=R\tilde{a}_{t-1}+z_{t}\\
 & \tilde{a}_{t}\geq0\\
\ln z_{t} & =\rho\ln z_{t-1}+\epsilon_{t}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then HH problem is independent of $p$ up to scale!
\begin{itemize}
\item Solution is ``scale independent'': $1\%$ more permanent income raises $c_{t}$ and $a_{t}$ by $1\%$ \pause
\item Homothetic preferences imply $\phi=1$, since $\tilde{c}_{t}=c_{t}/p$ \pause
\item Permanent redistribution has \emph{no effect} on aggregates: the lower saving of one group exactly offsets the higher saving of the other
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Non-homothetic HA model}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Extend standard HA model with\emph{ taste for wealth }(>>status<<)
\[
\begin{aligned}V\left(a_{t-1},z_{t},p\right)= & \max_{c_{t}}\frac{c_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}+\phi_{a}\frac{a_{t}^{1-\sigma_{a}}}{1-\sigma_{a}}+\beta\mathbb{E}\left[V\left(a_{t},z_{t+1},p\right)\right]\\
 & \text{ subject to }\\
 & c_{t}+a_{t}=a_{t-1}\left(1+r\right)+z_{t}p\\
 & a_{t}\geq0\\
\ln z_{t} & =\rho\ln z_{t-1}+\epsilon_{t}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item <+->Note: Still homothetic as long as $\sigma=\sigma_{a}$, but non-homothetic
if $\sigma\neq\sigma_{a}$:
\begin{align*}
\tilde{V}\left(\tilde{a}_{t-1},z_{t},p\right) & =\frac{\tilde{c}_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}+p^{\sigma-\sigma_{a}}\phi_{a}\frac{\tilde{a}_{t}^{1-\sigma_{a}}}{1-\sigma_{a}}+\beta\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{V}\left(\tilde{a}_{t},z_{t+1},p\right)\right]
\end{align*}
\item <+->If $\sigma\neq\sigma_{a}$, the weight $p^{\sigma-\sigma_{a}}$ on wealth depends on $p$: richer households put more weight on wealth when $\sigma>\sigma_{a}$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Applications}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Calibrate a life-cycle HA model with non-homothetic preferences
to estimate $\phi=0.7$
\begin{itemize}
\item Note: In paper there is a second source of non-homotheticity where
$\sigma$ varies across age 
\end{itemize}
\item <+->Segment HHs into 3 permanent income groups corresponding to poorest
90\%, next 9\% and richest 1\% 
\item <+->Feed in evolution of income inequality from Piketty and Saez
(2003), keeping aggregate income unchanged in PE (so permanent redistribution
between rich and poor HHs) \\
\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figs/Straub2019IncomeInequality.PNG}      
\end{figure}
\item <+->Solve for GE (Supply side as in HANC)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Results}
\begin{figure}
 \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/straub_2019_fig_6.png} 
\end{figure}

\end{frame}
\begin{frame}{GE implications of rising income inequality }
\begin{itemize}
\item Compare effects in homothetic and non-homothetic models: \\
\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.7\linewidth]{figs/Straub2019GE.PNG}      
\end{figure}
\end{itemize}
\begin{itemize}
\item Note: >>Fixed K<< is Lucas-tree economy, where wealth grows due to rising asset prices
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Trickle down economics?}

\begin{itemize}
\item In model with perfect competition: $\uparrow A \to \uparrow K \to \uparrow Y, w$ \pause
\item The GE effect benefits to everybody! \pause 
\item How realistic is this? Need to account for imperfect competition \pause
\item In this case: $r_t=\frac{\alpha}{\mu} K_t^{(\alpha-1)}-\delta$, and $q_t =\frac{p_{t+1}+q_{t+1}}{1+r_t}$ \pause
\item Increase in savings might not finance more physical capital, but just higher prices of financial assets!
\end{itemize} 
\end{frame}

\section[Asset supply and demand]{Asset supply and demand \\ Auclert, Malmberg, Rognlie and Straub (2025)}
\begin{frame}{The race between asset supply and asset demand}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Auclert, Malmberg, Rognlie and Straub (2025), AMRS below. The U.S. since 1950:
\begin{itemize}
\item fertility fell from over 3 children per woman to 1.6: the population ages
\item income inequality has risen sharply since the 1970s
\item government debt and the value of private assets rose, net foreign assets at a record low
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\item <+->Two questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item How did these shifts affect interest rates and wealth over the last 75 years?
\item What happens over the next 75 years, and what does it mean for public debt?
\end{enumerate}
\vfill
\item <+->Method: long-run asset supply and demand, measured with \emph{sufficient statistics} from a life-cycle model
\begin{itemize}
\item extends Auclert, Malmberg, Martenet and Rognlie (2024), who study demographics only
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Falling returns and rising wealth}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figs/AMRS_fig2.png}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
\item Average return $r=\bar{s}r^{f}+(1-\bar{s})r^{r}$: safe rate on government bonds $r^{f}$ and return on private assets $r^{r}$, with $\bar{s}=0.11$
\item Since the 1950s, $r$ fell by about 2 pp and wealth rose by about 300\% of GDP, mostly after 1980
\end{itemize}
{\footnotesize Source: AMRS (2025), Figure 2}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Realized asset supply and demand, 1950-2024}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figs/AMRS_fig3.png}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
\item Supply: government debt $B$, capital $K$, capitalized profits and rents $\Pi$. Demand: households $A^{h}$ and foreigners $-NFA$
\item $B$, $K$, $Y$ from the national accounts, $A^{h}$ and $NFA$ from the financial accounts, $\Pi$ as the residual
\item Supply rose through government debt and profits, demand through households and foreigners
\end{itemize}
{\footnotesize Source: AMRS (2025), Figure 3}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Asset market equilibrium}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->The long-run rate $r^{*}$ clears the market for assets, relative to GDP:
\[
\mathcal{A}^{s}(r^{*})=\mathcal{A}^{d}(r^{*})
\]
\item <+->\textbf{Asset supply}: domestic assets available to hold, decreasing in $r$ (less capital, profits worth less)
\[
\mathcal{A}^{s}=\underbrace{\frac{B}{Y}}_{\text{gov. debt}}+\underbrace{\frac{K}{Y}}_{\text{capital}}+\underbrace{\frac{\Pi}{Y}}_{\text{profits and rents}}
\]
\item <+->\textbf{Asset demand}: assets that households and foreigners want to hold, increasing in $r$
\[
\mathcal{A}^{d}=\underbrace{\frac{A^{h}}{Y}}_{\text{households}}+\underbrace{\left(-\frac{NFA}{Y}\right)}_{\text{foreigners}}
\]
\item <+->Vocabulary: household saving is a \emph{demand} for assets. Same diagram as Aiyagari (lectures 3-4), with $B$ and $\Pi$ added
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Measuring the shifts}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Let $\eta$ shift both curves, and define the semi-elasticities
\[
\epsilon^{s}\equiv-\frac{\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{s}}{\partial r}>0,\qquad\epsilon^{d}\equiv\frac{\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{d}}{\partial r}>0
\]
\item <+->Take logs of $\mathcal{A}^{s}(r^{*},\eta)=\mathcal{A}^{d}(r^{*},\eta)$ and differentiate:
\[
dr^{*}=\frac{\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{s}-\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{d}}{\epsilon^{s}+\epsilon^{d}},\qquad d\log\frac{A}{Y}=\frac{\epsilon^{d}\,\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{s}+\epsilon^{s}\,\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{d}}{\epsilon^{s}+\epsilon^{d}}
\]
where $\partial\log\mathcal{A}$ is the shift of a curve at a given $r$
\begin{itemize}
\item $r^{*}$ falls if and only if demand shifts more than supply
\end{itemize}
\item <+->Invert: the observed $dr$ and $d\log(A/Y)$ reveal the shifts
\[
\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{s}=d\log\frac{A}{Y}+\epsilon^{s}dr,\qquad\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{d}=d\log\frac{A}{Y}-\epsilon^{d}dr
\]
\item <+->Only two numbers needed: $\epsilon^{s}\approx20$ and $\epsilon^{d}\approx9$ (from the model below)
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Who won the race?}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figs/AMRS_fig1.png}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Asset supply shifts out: $A/Y$ up and $r^{*}$ up
\item <+->Asset demand shifts out: $A/Y$ up and $r^{*}$ down
\item <+->Data: $A/Y$ up and $r$ down $\Rightarrow$ asset demand won the race
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: overview}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Long run only: compare balanced growth paths, no transitions
\item <+->\textbf{Firms}: Cobb-Douglas, markup $\mu$, tax $\tau$ on income net of depreciation
\item <+->\textbf{Government}: debt $B$, consumption $G$, social security $T$, tax $\tau$ on all net income
\item <+->\textbf{Households}: overlapping generations (ages $j=0,\dots,J$) and permanent types $\theta$
\begin{itemize}
\item life-cycle consumption-saving problem, bequest motive, taxes and social security
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Two assets}: safe bonds ($r^{f}$) and risky private assets ($r^{r}$)
\begin{itemize}
\item risk premium $rp=r^{r}-r^{f}$ taken as given, households only care about the average return $r$
\end{itemize}
\item <+->Growth: $1+g=(1+n)(1+\gamma)$, with population growth $n$ and productivity growth $\gamma$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: asset supply}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Solve the firm's problem from the FOC: Cobb-Douglas, markup $\mu$, tax $\tau$ on profits net of depreciation. Capital FOC: $\frac{\alpha}{\mu}\frac{Y}{K}=\frac{r^{r}}{1-\tau}+\delta$, profits are a share $1-1/\mu$ of output
\item <+->Asset supply in closed form, with $r^{r}=r+\bar{s}\,rp$ the return on risky assets:
\[
\mathcal{A}^{s}(r)=\underbrace{\frac{\alpha}{\mu}\frac{1}{\frac{r^{r}}{1-\tau}+\delta}}_{K/Y\text{: capital}}+\underbrace{(1-\tau)(1+g)\frac{1-1/\mu}{r^{r}-g}}_{\Pi/Y\text{: value of profits and rents}}+\underbrace{\frac{B}{Y}}_{\text{gov. debt}}
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Pi/Y$: profits $(1-1/\mu)Y$ grow at $g$ and are discounted at $r^{r}$
\item $B/Y$: set by the government, does not respond to $r$
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\item <+->Semi-elasticity:
\[
\epsilon^{s}=\underbrace{\frac{K}{A}\frac{1}{r^{r}+(1-\tau)\delta}}_{\text{lower }r\text{: more capital}}+\underbrace{\frac{\Pi}{A}\frac{1}{r^{r}-g}}_{\text{lower }r\text{: rents worth more}}\approx20
\]
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: shifters of asset supply}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Public debt} $B/Y$: from the data. Going forward, aging raises deficits (pensions, health care)
\item <+->\textbf{Markups} $\mu$: less capital, but more profits to capitalize. With $r^{r}-g$ small, the second effect wins
\item <+->\textbf{Capital share} $\alpha$: technology (automation, AI), cheaper investment goods
\item <+->\textbf{Depreciation} $\delta$: shift toward short-lived capital (equipment, software) raises the user cost, less $K/Y$
\item <+->\textbf{Taxes} $\tau$: raise the user cost and lower after-tax profits
\item <+->\textbf{Growth} $1+g=(1+n)(1+\gamma)$: exogenous, from the data. Slower growth lowers the value of rents
\begin{itemize}
\item slower population growth $n$: the demographic effect on asset supply
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Risk premium} $rp$: at a given $r$, a higher $rp$ raises $r^{r}$: less capital, profits worth less
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: households}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Overlapping generations, each solving a deterministic life-cycle problem:
\[
\max_{\{\tilde{c}_{j},a_{j+1}\}}\sum_{j=0}^{J}\Phi_{j}\tilde{\beta}_{j}\frac{\tilde{c}_{j}^{1-1/\sigma}}{1-1/\sigma}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\tilde{c}_{j}+\phi_{j}a_{j+1}=y_{j}(\theta)+(1+r)a_{j}
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\phi_{j}$: survival probability from $j$ to $j+1$, $\Phi_{j}=\prod_{k<j}\phi_{k}$. Start with $a_{0}=0$
\item $\tilde{c}_{j}$: consumption, including end-of-life spending and bequests
\item $y_{j}(\theta)=(1-\tau)\,w\,\lambda(\theta)\left(\bar{e}_{j}+T\bar{t}_{j}\right)$: after-tax labor income and social security
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\item <+->Two sources of heterogeneity:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Age} $j$: income and wealth follow the life cycle
\item \textbf{Permanent income} $\lambda(\theta)$: scales the whole income profile
\end{enumerate}
No idiosyncratic income risk: the only risk is mortality
\vfill
\item <+->Preferences $\tilde{\beta}_{j}$ are set to match the observed profiles of consumption and wealth, by age and by income
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: households in the data}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Wealth by age and type} is read from the data, not computed:
\begin{itemize}
\item by age: 2016 profiles of net worth $a_{j}$ and labor income $we_{j}$ (SCF)
\item by type: $\theta$ is the percentile of labor income at ages 25-44, $\lambda(\theta)$ from DINA. In the PSID, log wealth on log labor income has a slope of 1.61, so $\bar{a}_{j}(\theta)=\bar{a}_{j}\lambda(\theta)^{0.61}$
\end{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Moments for $\epsilon^{d}$}, from $\pi_{j}$, $a_{j}$ and effective consumption $\tilde{c}_{j}$ (PSID consumption plus end-of-life spending):
\[
A^{h}=\sum_{j}\pi_{j}a_{j},\qquad\tilde{C}=\sum_{j}\pi_{j}\tilde{c}_{j},\qquad\mathbb{E}Age_{a}=\frac{\sum_{j}\pi_{j}a_{j}\,j}{A^{h}}
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}Age_{\tilde{c}}=\frac{\sum_{j}\pi_{j}\tilde{c}_{j}\,j}{\tilde{C}},\qquad\mathrm{Var}Age_{\tilde{c}}=\frac{\sum_{j}\pi_{j}\tilde{c}_{j}\left(j-\mathbb{E}Age_{\tilde{c}}\right)^{2}}{\tilde{C}}
\]
\item <+->\textbf{Interpretation}:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathbb{E}Age_{a}$: age of the owner of the average dollar of wealth
\item $\mathbb{E}Age_{\tilde{c}}$: age at which the average dollar is consumed
\item $\mathrm{Var}Age_{\tilde{c}}$: spread of consumption over the life cycle, the room to substitute
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{The slope of asset demand}
\begin{block}{Proposition 2 (with $r=g$)}
\[
\epsilon^{d}=\frac{1}{1+r}\Big(\underbrace{\sigma\frac{\tilde{C}}{(1+g)A^{h}}\mathrm{Var}Age_{\tilde{c}}}_{\text{substitution}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}Age_{\tilde{c}}-\mathbb{E}Age_{a}}_{\text{income}}\Big)
\]
$Age_{\tilde{c}}$, $Age_{a}$: age of a random unit of consumption or of wealth in the population
\end{block}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Depends only on the \textbf{age} structure of consumption and wealth, plus the EIS $\sigma$
\item <+->\textbf{Substitution} ($\sigma\times50.2$): a higher $r$ tilts consumption toward old age, so households save more when young
\item <+->\textbf{Income} ($-7.4$): wealth is about 7 years older than consumption. A higher return means less saving is needed for retirement
\item <+->With $\sigma=1/3$, $\epsilon^{d}\approx9$. Representative agent: $\epsilon^{d}=\infty$, so asset demand shifters cannot move $r^{*}$
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Model: shifters of asset demand}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->\textbf{Compositional}: change the weights on ages and types, not behavior. Reweight the 2016 data profiles
\begin{itemize}
\item $+$ \textbf{Demographics}: an older population puts more weight on asset-rich, low-income ages
\item $+$ \textbf{Productivity growth}: slower growth across cohorts makes older cohorts relatively richer, like aging
\item $+$ \textbf{Inequality}: income moves to the rich, who hold more wealth relative to their income, as in Straub (2019)
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\item <+->\textbf{Life-cycle}: change saving behavior, measured with first-order formulas
\begin{itemize}
\item $-$ \textbf{Social security}: more generous pensions, less saving for retirement
\item \textbf{Longevity}: dropped, since most assets are not annuitized
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\item <+->$+$ \textbf{Foreigners}: $-NFA/Y$ taken from the data
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Asset demand won the race}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{figs/AMRS_fig4.png}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Each year, two observations ($dr$, $d\log A/Y$ since 1950) and two unknown shifts:
\[
\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{s}=d\log\frac{A}{Y}+\epsilon^{s}dr,\qquad\partial\log\mathcal{A}^{d}=d\log\frac{A}{Y}-\epsilon^{d}dr
\]
change in $A/Y$ = shift of the curve + move along it caused by $dr$
\item <+->$r$ fell by about 2 pp. Along supply, $A/Y$ rises by $\epsilon^{s}\times0.02\approx40$ log points, most of the observed rise $\Rightarrow$ small supply shift
\item <+->Along demand, $A/Y$ falls by $\epsilon^{d}\times0.02\approx18$ log points, yet $A/Y$ rose $\Rightarrow$ large demand shift
\end{itemize}
{\footnotesize Source: AMRS (2025), Figure 4}
\end{frame}
%

\begin{itemize}
\item <+->Aging keeps raising asset demand: with fixed supply, $r^{*}$ falls by 1.2 pp by 2100
\item <+->But old-age spending rises from 11\% to 20\% of GDP: without adjustment, debt grows by 500\% of GDP and supply wins
\item <+->Debt stabilized in 2100 (figure): 250\% of GDP at today's $r$, but it needs an adjustment of about 12\% of GDP
\end{itemize}
{\footnotesize Source: AMRS (2025), Figure 15}
\end{frame}
%
\begin{frame}{Takeaways}
\begin{itemize}
\item <+->$r^{*}$ is set by a race between asset supply (debt, capital, profits) and asset demand (households, foreigners)
\item <+->Heterogeneity makes asset demand imperfectly elastic, so aging and inequality move $r^{*}$
\item <+->1950-2024: asset demand won by far (aging, inequality, slower growth, foreign inflows), and $r^{*}$ fell
\item <+->Going forward: aging raises asset demand, but also deficits. There is room to borrow, but a large fiscal adjustment is unavoidable
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\section[Indebted demand]{Indebted demand \\ Mian, Straub and Sufi (2021)}

\begin{frame}{Introduction}

\begin{itemize}
  \item Build on the non-homothetic preferences \pause 
  \item Highlights role of increasing household debt and connect to returns \pause 
\begin{figure}[H]     
\centering      
\includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figs/MSS2021Debt.PNG}      
\end{figure}
  \item Argue that income inequality and less financial regulation leads to more borrowing and lower returns in GE \pause
  \item \textbf{Note}: Would normally expect the opposite \pause
  \begin{itemize}
    \item If I want to borrow more, I will have to compensate savers by paying \textbf{higher} interest rate, not \textbf{lower} \pause
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Model}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Model \pause
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Continuous} time \pause
    \item Endowment economy with $Y=1$ \pause
  \end{itemize}
  \item Savers $s$ are unconstrained and maximize utility $$\int_0^\infty e^{-\rho t} \log (c_t^s)+\upsilon(a_t^s)dt$$ \pause
  \item Borrowers $b$ are constrained. They hold debt $d_t>0$ up to a share $\ell$ of collateral $p_t=\int_t^\infty e^{-rt} \omega^bYdt = \frac{\omega^b Y}{r}$ $$d_t =\frac{\ell\omega^b Y}{r}$$ \pause
  \item Equilibrium: debt owed by borrowing equal savings by savers: $$d_t =a_t^s$$  \pause
\end{itemize}  
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Non-homothetic model}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Calibration \pause
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Interpret savers at top 1\% of income distribution \pause
    \item Calibrate $\upsilon(a)$ such that savers have long-run MPC of 0.01 \pause
  \end{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Non-homotheticity}: Large differences in SR across the two types \pause
  \item Core insight of the paper: if savings is luxury good for rich, $\upsilon''(a_t^s)>0$, saving schedule $a_t^s(r)$ is \emph{downward sloping} \pause
  \begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figs/MSS2021DemandSupply.PNG} \pause
  \end{figure}
  \item Why? Assume rich agent consumes fixed amount $\bar{c}^s$ and saves the rest. Then $\bar{c}^s=r_ta_t^s\Leftrightarrow a_t^s = \frac{\bar{c}^s}{r_t}$ \pause
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Higher $r$ in the long run crowd out $a_t^s$ in the long run \pause
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Results}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Increase in income inequality: increase in debt and lower interest rates \pause
    \item Increase in financial deregulation $\to$ relax borrowing constraint: \\ more borrowing and lower interest rates \pause
    \begin{itemize}
      \item Note: standard GE argument would imply higher rates \pause
      \item Lower rates arise due to downward sloping savings schedule of rich savers\pause
    \end{itemize}

  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Results}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Increase in income inequality moves supply curve to the left \pause
    \item Inequality increases $\to$ saving by rich increase $\to$ lower $r$ $\to$ incentive to take more debt $d$ \pause
  \end{itemize}

  \begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figs/MSS2021Ineq.png}
  \end{figure}

\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Results - Monetary and fiscal policy}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A permanent increase in public debt due to deficit spending shock \pause
  \item Short run: $r$ increase to induce more saving by rich savers to finance gov. debt \pause
  \item Long run: the government pays $rB$ to savers, financed by lower $G$ or taxes on borrowers. Savers barely spend it, so demand falls and $r$ must fall. Lower $r$ crowds in household debt \pause
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figs/MSS2021Fiscal.PNG}
\end{figure} \pause
\item Opposite of AMRS, where more $B$ raises $r^{*}$: there asset demand slopes up ($\epsilon^{d}>0$), here the rich savers' demand slopes down \pause
\item For monetary policy: lower $r$ means ZLB more likely, ``less ammunition''
\end{itemize}  
\end{frame}
%

\section{Exercise}
\begin{frame}{Exercise}
\begin{itemize}
\item Consider the following PE HA model:
\[
\begin{aligned}V\left(a_{t-1},z_{t},p\right)= & \max_{c_{t}}\frac{c_{t}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}+\phi_{a}\frac{a_{t}^{1-\sigma_{a}}}{1-\sigma_{a}}+\beta\mathbb{E}\left[V\left(a_{t},z_{t+1},p\right)\right]\\
 & \text{ subject to }\\
 & c_{t}+a_{t}=a_{t-1}\left(1+r\right)+z_{t}p\\
 & a_{t}\geq0\\
\ln z_{t} & =\rho\ln z_{t-1}+\epsilon_{t}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item {\footnotesize\textbf{Q1}}{\footnotesize : Derive the Euler equation
of the model }{\footnotesize\par}

in }{\footnotesize\emph{household\_problem.py}}{\footnotesize{} with
the new Euler }{\footnotesize\par}

$\phi_{a}=0$, 2) $\phi_{a}=0.1,\sigma=\sigma_{a}=1$, 3) $\phi_{a}=0.1,\sigma=1,\sigma_{a}=0.7$}{\footnotesize\par}

you permanently redistribute resources across households (change $p$).
What are the aggregate effects across the models?}{\footnotesize\par}
\end{itemize}
